**On iPad, pre-rendered email readers are built at screen width and never adopted**

Area: iPad and iOS 17.6-25: devices and OS versions the app ships to and nothing runs. Verdict: corrected (medium confidence).

On iOS, visible rows pre-render an off-screen reader WebView at the scene's screen width. A checkout takes it only when that width equals the reader's GeometryReader width exactly. The app ships to iPad (all orientations, so multitasking applies), and there the reader is an unsized .sheet. In landscape, Split View, Slide Over or Stage Manager that sheet is narrower than the screen, so the row warms are never adopted. The prepared HTML has no width in its key and is still served. A prepaint at the measured width after an explicit open can still be adopted on a re-open, unless the row warms the message again at screen width first, which replaces that prepaint.

**Evidence**

- esc-chatmail/Platform/FullEmailReaderWarmWidthSource.swift:8-19 — iOS returns activeWindowScene()?.screen.bounds.width, documented as 'the width of the reader sheet on an iPhone'
- esc-chatmail.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj:262,282 — TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = "1,2", all four iPad orientations (Info.plist:142-148 the same), so iPad ships with multitasking
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/FullEmailReaderView.swift:19-26 with FullEmailReaderWebView.swift:28-34 — checkout width is the reader's GeometryReader width; ChatView.swift:172-179 and View+AppSheet.swift:40-44 present it as a plain sheet with no sizing
- esc-chatmail/Services/Chat/FullEmailWebViewManager.swift:1166-1181 — warm keeps an entry only on an exact key (width) match and otherwise tears it down and builds a new WebView; 1255-1279 explicit-open prepaint at the measured width likewise replaces the screen-width entry
- esc-chatmail/Services/Chat/FullEmailWebViewManager.swift:279-294 — FullEmailPreparedArtifactKey carries no width, so the prepared HTML payload still hits on iPad
- esc-chatmail/Services/Chat/FullEmailOpenSession.swift:430-463 — the measured width is recorded (only the Mac reads it) and a prepaint at that width is requested after an open

**Trigger.** Scrolling a chat that has HTML preview rows on an iPad in landscape, or in a Split View, Slide Over or Stage Manager window, then opening the full email. Portrait full-screen iPad depends on UIKit's page-sheet width and was not verified.

**Impact.** On iPad, every visible-row WebView pre-render is wasted work: one WKWebView load plus a snapshot per HTML row. At most 4 are kept by the LRU, the same work an iPhone does by design. A first open is a live render of the already-prepared HTML, behind the snapshot placeholder, not an instant adopted view. Each open also builds a second off-screen WebView at the sheet width. When the row warms again it is replaced at screen width, so adoption on re-open is unreliable. Mailbox size makes none of this worse.

**Verifier.** Every cited line matches the code today. There is no idiom or size-class guard: the kill switch is the only gate. The Mac plan (docs/mac-app-plan.md:302) and the iOS test keep screen width on iOS on the iPhone premise; nothing documents iPad. Corrections to the original claim: re-open adoption of the explicit-open prepaint still works; the churn is the same as iPhone's; the HTML is not cold. Severity is lowered because the cost is bounded and hidden behind the placeholder.

**October review.** docs/mac-app-plan.md:302 (iOS-to-Mac substitution table, warm-width row: records the Mac fix and leaves iOS on screen width; no iPad decision anywhere)

**Invariant risks**

- Reading lastMeasuredReaderWidth unkeyed on all of iOS breaks the iPhone. After a landscape open, portrait rows warm at the landscape width. Returning nil before a first open on every iOS device also drops the iPhone's first-open adoption. FullEmailReaderWarmWidthSourceTests.testCurrentWidth_onIOS_isTheSceneScreenWidthNotTheRecordedReaderWidth pins today's answer, so it has to be rewritten on purpose, with a Revert-check.
- Do not add width to FullEmailPreparedArtifactKey, and do not skip warm() when the width is nil. The prepared-HTML hit is the only warming benefit iPad gets today. Width belongs only in FullEmailWebViewPreRenderKey and in checkout's exact match.
- Keep checkout's exact width key. A width recorded during a rotation can be paired with the old scene size. Today that only costs a miss. With a width tolerance, a WebView laid out at another width would be adopted.
- Keep the UIKit reads (idiom, scene bounds) inside the #if canImport(UIKit) branch, and test a plain-value policy, or CI's Build (macOS) breaks. The AppKit branch and its Mac.xctestplan test stay unchanged. A new value type needs let properties or an explicit init: under Swift 6.2 a private var with a default makes the memberwise init private.

**Fix.** Leave the AppKit branch alone. FullEmailReaderWarmWidthSource records the measured width with the scene size it was measured in (scene.coordinateSpace.bounds.size). Its iOS decision moves to a pure policy that takes plain values: the recorded width and scene size, the current scene size, the screen width, and isPhone. On iOS it returns the recorded width when the scene size still matches. Otherwise it returns the screen width on a phone, which is today's iPhone behaviour, and nil anywhere else. With nil, iPad warms prepared HTML only, which warm() already does at lines 1152-1156. Keep the prepared key free of width and keep the exact checkout match. Update the 'only the Mac reads it' comments and mac-app-plan.md:302.

**First step.** Move the iOS branch of FullEmailReaderWarmWidthSource.currentWidth into a pure FullEmailReaderWarmWidthPolicy function over plain values, with no change in behaviour. Pin today's iPhone answer in a test that imports no UIKit.

**Pinning test.** FullEmailReaderWarmWidthPolicyTests covers: iPad, unmeasured → nil; iPad, measured in the same scene size → measured width; scene resized → nil; iPhone, unmeasured → screen width. Plus a manager test that a row re-warm keeps the explicit-open prepainted WebView.

**Payoff.** On iPad, re-opens adopt a painted reader instead of rendering live. No WebView pre-renders are wasted before a first open, and row re-warms stop replacing the explicit-open prepaint.

### `gap-ipad-and-os-floor#6` · low · reliability · effort S · new

**iOS image attachments are capped by screen width, with no clamp to the window**

Area: iPad and iOS 17.6-25: devices and OS versions the app ships to and nothing runs. Verdict: corrected (medium confidence).

On iOS a single image reserves a fixed frame of min(0.65 × UIScreen width, 280) pt. That is the screen's width, and .standard has no transcript clamp. On iPhone the window is the screen, so the cap always fits. On iPad (universal, multitasking on, no iPad layout) a 320-pt window still caps at 280. An incoming row needs 24 + 8 + 280 + 8 + the Spacer's minimum, about 320–328 pt, against 288 pt of content width, so it overflows by about 32–40 pt. Outgoing rows overflow by about 8–16 pt.

**Evidence**

- esc-chatmail/Views/Components/Attachments/ImageAttachmentBubble.swift:18-20 — maxWidth = styleMaxWidth ?? min(PlatformScreen.width * 0.65, MessageBubbleStyle.standard.maxBubbleWidth); the frame is fixed (ImageAttachmentLayout scales a photo to the full cap)
- esc-chatmail/Platform/PlatformScreen.swift:25-31 — UIScreen.main.bounds.width on iOS, 'so every iPhone keeps its bubble widths' (iPad is not considered)
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/MessageBubble.swift:232-237, 283, 300-302, 599-607 — HStack spacing 8, the avatar slot, the column frame(maxWidth: 280), a trailing Spacer; for .standard imageAttachmentMaxWidth is nil
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ChatMessagesView.swift:429 — .padding(.horizontal) on the LazyVStack; MessageBubbleRowPolicy.swift:21-24 — .standard shows the 24-pt avatar or placeholder in 1:1 chats too
- esc-chatmail.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj:282 — TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = "1,2"; esc-chatmail/Resources/Info.plist:142-148 — all four iPad orientations and no UIRequiresFullScreen, so Slide Over and Split View are available
- esc-chatmailTests/Chat/MessageBubbleStyleTests.swift:8-11, 150-156 — pins that the iPhone's .standard does not move and that its imageMaxWidth(transcriptWidth:) is nil at every width

**Trigger.** iPad only: a 320-pt Slide Over window or a narrow Split View pane showing a chat with a single photo attachment. The bug does not occur on an iPhone: with a 320-pt Display Zoom screen the cap becomes 208 and the row fits.

**Impact.** An incoming photo row is wider than its 288-pt slot by about 32–40 pt. Centred by the stack, the avatar reaches or crosses the window's leading edge and the photo runs into the trailing margin. The effect is cosmetic: nothing is lost, and no other rows change.

**Verifier.** Opened every cited site. There is no horizontalSizeClass or userInterfaceIdiom handling anywhere, and no documented iPad decision. Multi-image grids use flexible columns and shrink, so only a single image is fixed. I dropped the iPhone rotation claim: the screen-relative cap is the deliberate, pinned iPhone design, and rotation lays out the transcript again anyway. The recommendation also changes. Removing PlatformScreen.width would move iPhone widths and break the pinned rule. Instead, clamp: min(currentCap, transcriptWidth − 48). That leaves every iPhone unchanged and fixes narrow iPad windows. Nothing was rendered.

**October review.** docs/mac-imessage-ui-plan.md "PR 4 as built (2026-11-12)" Width bullet (Mac-only clamp precedent); no iPad item in docs/scalability-review.md

**Invariant risks**

- The iPhone's .standard must not move (MessageBubbleStyleTests.swift:8-11, CLAUDE.md, mac-imessage-ui-plan PR 4). The recommended min(280, room) drops the 0.65 screen share, so images on 375-pt and 393-pt iPhones grow from 243.75 and 255.45 pt to 280 pt, and every image row's reserved height changes.
- Routing the clamp through .standard.imageMaxWidth(transcriptWidth:) breaks its pinned nil (MessageBubbleStyleTests.swift:45, 150-156). It also feeds \.imageAttachmentMaxWidth (MessageBubble.swift:604-607), and that would replace the screen-share cap outright in ImageAttachmentBubble.swift:19.
- Rows must not change height after they mount (AGENTS.md:139; the reveal note in mac-imessage-ui-plan). Tying the share to the viewport everywhere makes every image row resize on rotation or an iPad resize. Clamp only where room is short, as the Mac does, and treat a width of 0 or a non-finite width as no clamp.
- Keep PlatformScreen.width: .compact.maxBubbleWidth and IOSPlatformShimTests use it. It is @MainActor, so pass the screen width into a nonisolated pure function to avoid CI's Swift 6.2 isolation errors. Never put the width into MessageBubbleLoadSignatureComponents or a .task id.

**Fix.** Keep the iPhone formula and add only a clamp. Add a pure, nonisolated function, MessageBubbleStyle.standardImageMaxWidth(screenWidth:transcriptWidth:). It returns min(0.65 × screen, 280), lowered to max(120, transcriptWidth − 96) only where that is smaller. A width of 0 or a non-finite width means no clamp. A new environment value, set in MessageBubble.attachmentsView beside imageAttachmentMaxWidth, carries transcriptWidth. ImageAttachmentBubble.maxWidth becomes styleMaxWidth ?? that function, passing PlatformScreen.width. Leave .standard.imageMaxWidth(transcriptWidth:) nil and the Mac path untouched. The clamp bites only below 274 pt of iPhone width (no iPhone is that narrow) and below 376 pt on iPad. The 96-pt chrome covers an iPad default padding that has not been measured.

**First step.** Write the pure width function and its number test in MessageBubbleStyleTests, then carry the transcript width from MessageBubble.attachmentsView to ImageAttachmentBubble through a new environment key.

**Pinning test.** MessageBubbleStyleTests, screen/transcript in: 320/320→208, 375/375→243.75, 393/393→255.45, 852/734→280 (no change); 1024/320→224; 1024/0 and 1024/∞→280. Revert-check: remove the clamp. Plus mount ImageAttachmentBubble in ImageAttachmentBubbleLayoutTests at transcript width 320.

**Payoff.** Single-photo rows fit in iPad Slide Over and narrow Split View windows, and no iPhone row moves, so the iOS before/after redraw stays identical. The gain is cosmetic and low priority.

### `mac-platform#5` · low · reliability · effort S · new

**Fail-closed latches and per-launch state assume a process that restarts often; a Mac process lives for days**

Area: macOS target architecture and platform shim layer. Verdict: corrected (high confidence).

The latches cannot be reached with today's code. Every close waits for all of its work with no timeout, and nothing new can register while admission is closed, so each reopen guard finds the registry empty. The credential park is lifted by any successful sign-in, and revoked credentials need one anyway. The list-limit point was already in the prior review. What remains is a cosmetic gap: Mac sidebar row timestamps are worked out only when a row is drawn, so after midnight an unchanged row keeps showing yesterday's time until it redraws.

**Evidence**

- esc-chatmail/Services/Send/OutboundTaskRegistry.swift:118-124,237-251 — reserve() refuses while admission is closed; cancelAndAwaitAll waits with no timeout until entries is empty. AuthSession.swift:549-553 and :679-683 run that drain and cleanupDownloads before any reopen.
- esc-chatmail/Services/Attachments/AttachmentAccountWorkRegistry.swift:64-65,114-118,149-163,169-171 — new work is refused while closed and the drain awaits every task, so the reopen guard's operations.isEmpty always holds afterwards. AttachmentDownloader.swift:513-529 has the same shape.
- esc-chatmail/Services/Preview/EmailPreviewSnapshotRenderer.swift:130,193-195,308-329 — starts open; enqueue refuses a closed generation; close awaits every task and then empties allWorkByID and runningCount. FullEmailWebViewManager.swift:1087-1091,1557-1561: warm() refuses while closed, and close waits for warm operations to drain.
- esc-chatmail/Services/Security/AuthSession.swift:425-436,659-660,707-708 — the launch reopen runs with no close before it, but both pools start open, so a refused reopen leaves them open. Both places that publish a session call pendingActionAuthenticationDidRecover. PendingActionsManager.swift:377-406 lifts the park there.
- docs/scalability-review.md:794-804 — the growing loadedConversationLimit is already the prior item conversation-list-window-full-refetch, and it is not specific to the Mac.
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ConversationRowView.swift:169-170 + esc-chatmail/Utilities/TimestampFormatter.swift:22-31 — the Today/Yesterday/weekday label is computed when the body runs, and MacConversationSidebar.swift:113-121 uses this row. docs/mac-imessage-ui-plan.md:397 records the same redraw-time behavior as accepted for the chat's time lines only.

**Trigger.** The Mac app stays open past midnight, and sidebar rows whose snapshot has not changed are not redrawn.

**Impact.** Visible rows with no new mail keep the wrong label after midnight, which is cosmetic. A row from 11:40 PM still reads "11:40 PM" the next morning, so it looks like today's mail, until the row is redrawn or new mail reaches it. Nothing stops working: sending, downloads, previews and the queued Gmail actions are not affected.

**Verifier.** I read every cited latch and traced its close path. Each drain awaits all of its tasks, and admission blocks new work while closed, so no work from the old account can reach reopen. The comments describe defensive guards, not states that can happen. A task that never finishes would hang the transition itself, on iOS as on the Mac; the finding does not claim that. Revoked credentials need a sign-in, and a sign-in runs the recovery hook. The list limit is a prior item. Only the sidebar timestamp gap holds, and the docs accept the same behavior for chat time lines.

**October review.** docs/mac-imessage-ui-plan.md:397 accepts a label worked out at redraw time for the chat's time lines only, not the sidebar. The list-window part that was dropped is docs/scalability-review.md:796 conversation-list-window-full-refetch (step 11, not built).

**Invariant risks**

- MacSystemLifecycleObserver.start keeps one handler, and a later call replaces it (MacSystemLifecycleObserver.swift:17-21). Routing the day clock through it would silently take the wake and activation events away from the foreground sync session that esc_chatmailApp.swift:267 starts.
- Two ways of redrawing the rows break the rows' Equatable short-circuit: reloading the window (reloadConversationWindowFromStore), or putting 'now' into ConversationSnapshot or ConversationListItem. Either one repeats the full re-snapshot of every row on the main thread (conversation-list-window-full-refetch). Keep publishVisibleItems as the one funnel and never add an FRC.
- Set the value on the sidebar's List, not at the NavigationSplitView root. MacMailboxDetail is .equatable() (MacMailboxView.swift:92) so that list publishes do not re-evaluate the transcript, whose rows must not change after mount. Any new state in MacConversationSidebar must be a property wrapper, not a plain private var (the CI Swift 6.2 memberwise-init trap).
- The finding suggests two more fixes; build neither. An automatic retry of a refused reopen outside AuthSession's FIFO transition gate breaks the all-or-none reopen and the split between .latchedRefusal and .supersededByAccountRemoval, so a retry could publish a session that a queued sign-out owns. Re-running the launch repairs outside a sync run breaks the rule that contact links are adopted in one place (refreshIfNeeded).

**Fix.** Build only the timestamp part: the latches are unreachable, and trimming the list window belongs to step 11's keyset paging. Add a @MainActor CalendarDayClock (ObservableObject) that publishes the current day's start only when it changes. It recomputes on NSCalendarDayChanged, NSSystemClockDidChange, NSSystemTimeZoneDidChange and its own wake and activation observations, never through MacSystemLifecycleObserver.start. Hold it as a @StateObject in MacMailboxView and ConversationListView, and set an environment value on the sidebar's List and the iOS list only. ConversationRowView reads it and passes it to a new TimestampFormatter.format(_:now:), whose output is otherwise unchanged. Snapshots, the list store and the chat time lines stay as they are.

**First step.** Add a now: parameter (defaulting to Date()) to TimestampFormatter.format. Then add a CalendarDayClock that takes an injected NotificationCenter, calendar and clock, with its unit tests, before touching ConversationRowView or either list.

**Pinning test.** CalendarDayClockTests: once the injected clock passes midnight, a posted NSCalendarDayChanged publishes one new day, and an activation on the same day publishes nothing. A repositorySource pin checks that ConversationRowView passes the environment day to TimestampFormatter.format(_:now:).

**Payoff.** Sidebar and iOS list timestamps stay correct across midnight, time-zone changes and wake. The cost is one re-evaluation of the rows on screen per day change, with no fetch and no snapshot rebuild.

### `mac-platform#6` · low · maintainability · effort S · new

**Private-structure hooks and the sandbox signal fail silently, and one of them fails into a wedge**

Area: macOS target architecture and platform shim layer. Verdict: corrected (medium confidence).

Only the sandbox part holds. `SandboxTripwirePolicy` takes `APP_SANDBOX_CONTAINER_ID` as its only proof of the sandbox. If a sandboxed process ever lacked that variable, account removal would throw and keep its reset marker. Every later sign-in then reruns `performDurableLocalCleanup` and throws `localAccountIsolationFailed`, so one sign-out locks the account out for good. That cost falls on sandboxed users, beyond the documented one for unsandboxed builds. No macOS release is known to drop the variable. The other hooks have documented fallbacks, have narrow impact, or are pinned by Mac-plan tests. The "unbounded KVO" claim is wrong: the handler writes only on true, so its own write ends the chain.

**Evidence**

- esc-chatmail/Services/Security/SandboxTripwirePolicy.swift:23,37-43 — `APP_SANDBOX_CONTAINER_ID` missing or blank means `.refusedOutsideAppSandbox`; nothing else is checked
- esc-chatmail/Services/Security/AuthSession.swift:908-913,1636-1644,1984-1991 — the attachment cleanup throws the tripwire refusal, `performDurableLocalCleanup` throws before clearing `localStoreResetRequired`, and the failure path keeps the marker
- esc-chatmail/Services/Security/AuthSession.swift:1191-1200,1237-1242 — with the marker held, every sign-in or restore reruns the cleanup and throws `localAccountIsolationFailed`, so the account stays locked out
- esc-chatmail/Services/Security/MacUnitTestHostPolicy.swift:45 and MacUnitTestHostGuard.swift:22-31 — the same variable gates the Mac test host, which logs the reason and exits, so any Mac-plan run on an OS without the variable fails loudly (CI runs no Mac tests)
- esc-chatmail/Platform/MacSidebarCollapseGuardView.swift:29-31,69-72 — the handler writes only when `canCollapse` is true, so its own write does not re-enter; with no item found, the documented fallback `MacSidebarVisibilityPolicy.correction` (MacSidebarVisibilityPolicy.swift:49-51) reopens the sidebar
- esc-chatmailTests/Platform/MacMainWindowCloseObserverTests.swift:53-60 — the 'main' identifier is read from the test host's real app window; esc-chatmail/Platform/SignOutMenuAction.swift:47 — `FocusedWindowSheet` (not identifier-based) covers the focused window, so the identifier matters only when the Settings window is in front

**Trigger.** A future macOS (or a launch path) in which a properly sandboxed MushMail process lacks `APP_SANDBOX_CONTAINER_ID`, followed by a sign-out or an account switch. No such release is known. The variable was measured as set in this app's sandboxed launch (docs/mac-app-plan.md:382), and the fresh-install cleanup ran with no refusal (line 399).

**Impact.** In that case a sign-out leaves the reset marker behind and no later sign-in or restore can publish a session, so the Mac app stays locked out until a build changes. With the variable missing, orphan sweeps and backup marks would also be skipped without anything telling the user. The other hooks fail into narrow, documented fallbacks. Closing the window with Settings open would no longer quit; SwiftUI's own quit on the last `Window` still applies otherwise. Signing out from the Settings window over a compose sheet would no longer be refused. Without the collapse guard, the visibility reset still reopens the sidebar, and without the list guard, the fill still covers the table's own selection.

**Verifier.** I opened every cited location and the sign-out → sign-in path. The wedge is real in code but rests on a hypothetical OS change. The choice of signal is documented (mac-app-plan.md:224, 382), and the Mac test host guard is a loud canary. The window-identifier, list and split-view hooks are recorded as HONEST SCOPE and have fallbacks. The KVO handler cannot loop by itself, unlike the table guard, whose write reloads the table. So severity drops to low, and the finding narrows to one point: a second public sandbox signal (entitlement through SecTask, or a home directory under Containers) would remove the single point of failure.

**October review.** docs/mac-app-plan.md PR C "Sandbox tripwire" (line 224: env var given only "for example"; line 382: measured set). Not in docs/scalability-review.md (lines 1572/1578 only reuse the tripwire).

**Invariant risks**

- Local-store isolation (CLAUDE.md account boundary; AuthSession.swift:1609-1644, 1984-1991, 1237-1242): 'unwedging' by treating a tripwire refusal as success or clearing localStoreResetRequired would publish a new account over the old account's surviving bodies and attachments.
- Fail-closed tripwire (SandboxTripwirePolicy.swift:34-36; CLAUDE.md 'Never launch an unsandboxed Mac build'): a scheme or test plan can set HOME/NSHomeDirectory or environment variables in an unsigned host (MacUnitTestHostPolicyTests.swift:26-28), so a proof read from them can be faked. Requiring both proofs (AND) would lock out today's users if SecTask misreads.
- Source pins: SandboxTripwireTests.swift:21-36,131-142 require byte-identical guard statements and an exact count of tripwire calls outside SandboxTripwire* files. BackupExclusionTests.swift:88-96 pins marksFiles' verdict line, so that test changes in the same commit.
- Mac.xctestplan:90,107-108 runs the SandboxTripwire* and MacUnitTestHostPolicy tests in a host that really is sandboxed. If the pure policy defaults to reading the real entitlement, every refusal test that injects an 'unsandboxed' environment permits there. Separately, a lifetime cap on canCollapse writes would break the guard, which SwiftUI resets at every update (MacSidebarCollapseGuardView.swift:22-24).

**Fix.** Keep the tripwire fail-closed and the reset-marker lockout; widen only what counts as proof. Add a pure `SandboxEvidence` (environment, hasSandboxEntitlement) and have `destructiveCleanupVerdict(evidence:)` permit on a non-blank `APP_SANDBOX_CONTAINER_ID` OR the signed `com.apple.security.app-sandbox` entitlement (SecTaskCopyValueForEntitlement on SecTaskCreateFromSelf, read once, macOS only), the proof verify-mac-test-host.sh already trusts. No home-directory heuristic (HOME and test-plan env are spoofable), no AND. Thread `evidence: = .current` through SandboxTripwire, BackupExclusion.marksFiles and MacUnitTestHostPolicy so every guard statement stays byte-identical; log once when the proofs disagree. Skip the telemetry event (NoopTelemetryClient) and any lifetime cap on canCollapse writes.

**First step.** In a throwaway Mac program (never the app), measure SecTaskCopyValueForEntitlement(SecTaskCreateFromSelf(nil), "com.apple.security.app-sandbox") when signed with ENABLE_APP_SANDBOX versus unsigned, and whether APP_SANDBOX_CONTAINER_ID is set in each, on macOS 27.2.

**Pinning test.** SandboxTripwirePolicyTests: no container ID plus entitlement gives .permitted (Revert-check: the entitlement disjunct); neither gives a refusal. Existing refusal tests inject hasSandboxEntitlement: false so they hold in the sandboxed Mac host. A Mac-plan test checks that SandboxEvidence.current reports the entitlement.

**Payoff.** Removes the single point of failure that would lock every sandboxed Mac user out after one sign-out on an OS that drops the variable, without weakening the unsandboxed-build refusal.

## Accessibility (6)

### `gap-accessibility-architecture#1` · medium · reliability · effort M · new

**Transcript rows have no accessibility model: a message is several unrelated VoiceOver stops, with no sender, direction or unread state**

Area: Accessibility under a virtualized transcript and fixed-height layout contracts. Verdict: corrected (medium confidence).

The mechanism holds. Neither MessageBubble nor ConversationRowView groups or labels its parts, so each Text and Button is its own VoiceOver stop, and nothing says who sent a message. Direction shows only in layout and color. In an iOS one-to-one chat, incoming rows get only an initials avatar, and only on the last row of a run. Mac one-to-one rows have no avatar at all. Unread is an unlabeled Circle. That matters mainly in the mailbox list, because opening a chat marks it read. The claim about the reveal stealing focus is not supported.

**Evidence**

- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/MessageBubble.swift:232-303 — leadingContent, senderNameView, subjectView, attachmentsView, MessageContentView and metadataLine are siblings in an HStack/VStack; the only accessibility modifiers in the file are on the recovery badge (524-525)
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/MessageBubbleRowPolicy.swift:21-24,35 — avatar only where endsRun (else a clear placeholder), none for .mac one-to-one; sender name only in groups. InitialsAvatarView.swift:103 — avatar is a bare Text(initials)
- esc-chatmail/Views/Components/MessageMetadata.swift:11-14 — unread is a 6pt Circle with no label; ChatMessagesCoordinator.swift:510-512 marks the conversation read on appear, so this dot is transient in a transcript
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ConversationRowView.swift:127-134 — mailbox unread is an unlabeled Circle; ConversationListView.swift:93-102 opens the row via onTapGesture on a plain view, not a Button/NavigationLink, so nothing combines its texts
- git grep esc-chatmail/ — accessibilityElement only at GoogleDriveSharedFileCardView.swift:27; no AccessibilityFocusState, accessibilityAction or accessibilityRotor
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ChatMessagesView.swift:393 — Reply/Forward/View original exist as the row's .contextMenu; 657-661 the labeled spinner; 169 transcript accessibilityHidden while covered

**Trigger.** Using a chat transcript or the mailbox list with VoiceOver on, on either platform.

**Impact.** A VoiceOver user hears several stops per message: initials, subject, the bubble as a button, and the timestamp. None of them says the sender or whether the user wrote it. Mid-run rows in a one-to-one chat, and every row of a Mac one-to-one chat, give no direction cue at all. In the mailbox list, unread conversations cannot be told apart from read ones. This shuts out one group of users. It is not a scale, data or reliability failure.

**Verifier.** I opened every cited location. No grouping or label modifier is applied anywhere on the row's path, and no document records a decision to defer accessibility. Four corrections to the original claim. The transcript's unread dot is transient because opening the chat marks it read. The reveal-focus claim assumes VoiceOver was on the spinner, which the code cannot show. The row already offers Reply, Forward and View original through its contextMenu. Severity is lowered to medium: VoiceOver is not one of the rubric's common conditions, and nothing here is lost or corrupted. The VoiceOver behavior described is inferred from SwiftUI's defaults; nobody has listened to it.

**October review.** CLAUDE.md Traps, MessageFieldPolicy note: "A test host is told nothing of SwiftUI's own accessibility… VoiceOver has not been heard on either platform" (no row item in docs/scalability-review.md)

**Invariant risks**

- Row height and identity. An accessibility-only child added inside MessageBubble's VStack (spacing 4) or inside ConversationRowView's stacks adds height after mount and changes the pinned .standard/.iOS pixels. A modifier wrapped in an `if` creates _ConditionalContent and remounts rows (ConversationListView.swift:80-88) along with their onAppear/onDisappear realization evidence (ChatMessagesView.swift:396-418). Use only modifiers, applied unconditionally.
- Focus on reveal. AccessibilityFocusState makes VoiceOver scroll to its target, which fights ChatMessagesCoordinator's hidden anchor pass and bottom-follow. On the Mac it would also take focus from the sidebar's arrow keys and the reply field (focusesFieldWhenChatAppears, ChatComposerFocus). The transcript is already accessibilityHidden while it is covered (ChatMessagesView.swift:169).
- Content drift. A label rebuilt from ChatMessageRowModel's chatPreviewText, bodyText or subject re-derives what MessageContentView.resolvedVisibleText (305-314), MessageDisplayPolicy and the stored rich verdict decide. It would read stripped share links, card text or the Loading pill wrongly. Let .combine take the children's own text and the cards' existing labels.
- Combine scope. Combining at the row in ChatMessagesView would swallow the Mac time line's isHeader (ChatTranscriptRowLeadIn.swift:16-22, ChatTimestampSeparator.swift:32). It could also merge the bubble Button, which opens the reader or the failed-send dialog (MessageContentView.swift:151-176), with the recovery badge (MessageBubble.swift:516-525) into one activation. Joining labels with Text + Text fails the Mac build (MessageBubble.swift:492-493).

**Fix.** Mailbox first. ConversationRowView has no controls, so put `.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)` on rowContent. Its label comes from a pure ConversationRowAccessibilityPolicy fed the body's own resolved displayName, unread count, pinned state, date and snippet. Add the isButton and isSelected traits on the iOS row, applied unconditionally. Transcript second. A pure MessageRowAccessibilityPolicy gives only the speaker ("You" or the sender), the existing status label and the time, never content text. Hide the avatar and the sender-name Text. Combine only MessageBubble's inner column, with the policy's text as an interpolated label prefix (iOS 18+ and Mac) or as accessibilityCustomContent on iOS 17. Leave the recovery badge separate. Drop focus-on-reveal.

**First step.** Add ConversationRowAccessibilityPolicy as a pure enum and apply its label with `.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)` on ConversationRowView's rowContent, reusing the displayName the body already resolves. Test the policy in a suite that Mac.xctestplan also lists.

**Pinning test.** Two pure suites. ConversationRowAccessibilityPolicyTests: unread and pinned are spoken. MessageRowAccessibilityPolicyTests: a mid-run Mac one-to-one row names its sender, an own row says "You" and "Not sent", no body text. Plus repositorySource pins and Revert-check comments.

**Payoff.** VoiceOver users get one stop per message that says who wrote it and its send state, and can tell unread conversations apart in the mailbox. No data, scale or reliability gain.

### `gap-accessibility-architecture#2` · medium · reliability · effort M · new

**Arrivals and send outcomes are announced to no one, yet arrivals are marked read in Gmail on visual geometry**

Area: Accessibility under a virtualized transcript and fixed-height layout contracts. Verdict: corrected (high confidence).

The app never posts an accessibility announcement. While a chat's scene and window are active, no sheet or alert is up, and the 1pt bottom anchor sits in the viewport, a newly arrived message is marked read. A reply that fails before transmission is kept as "Not sent", and send() still returns normally, so no alert is raised. A later ambiguous or rejected outcome only changes the caption and badge. VoiceOver users therefore hear neither arrivals nor the change into a failed state. The failed state does stay on the bubble, labeled for VoiceOver.

**Evidence**

- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ChatMessagesCoordinator.swift:653-680 — handleLatestWindowLayout marks pending arrivals read when the chat is ready, visible, active and uncovered, showing the latest window, and the bottom anchor is visible
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ChatView.swift:332-355 — isChatActiveAndUncovered is scene, window, sheet and alert state, documented as 'Whether someone can be looking at this chat'
- esc-chatmail/ViewModels/ChatViewModel.swift:1013,1045-1053 — the field is cleared at tap, and a non-nil result returns with no sendErrorAlert (the alert at 1137-1139 is raised only on the rollback path)
- esc-chatmail/Services/Send/OutboundMessageCoordinator.swift:203-206 — send returns after admission, or once a .retainAsNotSent pre-barrier failure has been kept as Not sent
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/MessageBubble.swift:516-525 — the recovery badge is a Button with accessibilityLabel(prompt.title) ('Not Sent'/'Delivery Unknown', FailedSendRecoveryPolicy.swift:45-58) and a hint, so the state is there for VoiceOver to find
- git grep in esc-chatmail/ for AccessibilityNotification, UIAccessibility.post, NSAccessibility.post, isVoiceOverRunning, sensoryFeedback and UNUserNotificationCenter — no matches

**Trigger.** A VoiceOver user has a chat open and resting at its newest row when mail arrives, or when a reply they sent becomes Not sent or Delivery unknown (offline wait timeout, background expiry, ambiguous error).

**Impact.** An arrival nobody announced is marked read in Gmail. It is still in the open transcript, and the read flag can be undone (ChatViewModel.toggleMessageRead). A failed or uncertain reply is not announced when it fails. The user finds out only by moving to that bubble, where the badge and hint say it. Nothing is lost and no state is wrong: this is an accessibility gap.

**Verifier.** I confirmed every cited location. The severity is lowered from high: no mail or reply is lost; an arrival stays in the open transcript; read state can be undone; the failed state persists and VoiceOver can reach it (labeled badge, hint, "View send error" menu item at ChatMessagesView.swift:1004). A sighted user who is not looking meets the same auto-read heuristic. Related, not limited to accessibility: the conversation list shows no failed-send marker, so a sighted user who leaves the chat mid-send also gets no notice. Nothing in the docs records this as a deliberate decision.

**Invariant risks**

- Non-idempotent send outcome matrix: do not raise an alert or change send()'s return for .retainAsNotSent (OutboundMessageCoordinator.swift:203-206), and do not route announcements through OutboundMessageReconciliationHooks. ChatViewModel outlives its screen (ChatReplyComposerDirectory), so a hook would speak about a chat that is not on screen.
- isChatActiveAndUncovered also gates the transcript's inset shifts (ChatBottomInsetPolicy.swift:263-281, ChatView.swift:332-333). Adding a VoiceOver term there changes keyboard and inset behavior. Skipping auto-read for VoiceOver users would leave Gmail read state and the unread badges different for those users, which is a product decision.
- Echo swap and mapper fallback: diff on ChatMessageDisplayIdentity, not on objectID or id. Announce only a change out of .sending, never on mount or window loads. MessageSendStatusLinePolicy.Line depends on per-row view state (isSendingRevealDue, isNewestInTranscript), and the mapper falls back to .none when a record fetch fails.
- Read changes merge in from a background context (MessageActions). Build the announcement text synchronously in the same main-actor turn from ChatMessageRowModel values. No delayed Task that could speak old-account content after teardown, no body-file reads, never log the text. Add no hand-reset stored state to ChatMessagesCoordinator.

**Fix.** Change only the view layer. Leave Services/Send and the read gate alone. Add a pure ChatTranscriptAnnouncementPolicy and an injected ChatAnnouncer: the production one posts AccessibilityNotification.Announcement, and tests record instead. Arrivals: markUnreadInboxMessagesAsReadIfNeeded returns the IDs it marks, and handleLatestWindowLayout announces exactly those, in the same turn, built from ChatMessageRowModel values, one announcement per layout. Send outcomes: ChatMessagesView observes, with onChange, a derived [displayIdentity: MessageSendStatusPresentation] for own rows. It announces only .sending changing to notSent, deliveryUnknown or sendFailed, gated on isChatActiveAndUncovered. Do not diff on Line or objectID. Whether auto-read should skip VoiceOver users stays the owner's decision.

**First step.** Add esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ChatTranscriptAnnouncementPolicy.swift, with sendOutcomeAnnouncements(old:new:) over [ChatMessageDisplayIdentity: MessageSendStatusPresentation] and arrivalAnnouncement(rows:), plus its XCTest suite. Then inject the announcer into ChatMessagesCoordinator as a defaulted closure.

**Pinning test.** Policy tests: .sending changing to notSent, deliveryUnknown or sendFailed announces once. nil→notSent, none→notSent and sending→none (the echo) do not. ChatMessagesCoordinatorTests (near line 1174): the announce closure receives exactly the IDs that were marked read, and neither closure runs while uncovered. Each test carries a Revert-check.

**Payoff.** VoiceOver users hear new mail before it is marked read in Gmail, and hear a reply become Not sent or Delivery unknown. Send semantics, read rules and layout do not change.

### `gap-accessibility-architecture#5` · medium · maintainability · effort S · new

**iOS icon-only controls and list rows carry no accessible names or traits, while their Mac counterparts do**

Area: Accessibility under a virtualized transcript and fixed-height layout contracts. Verdict: corrected (high confidence).

The real split is between shared components and views written for one place, not between iOS and Mac. The shared SendButton and DraftAttachmentThumbnail have no accessibility names, and the Mac uses both of them too: its New Message sheet sends through SendButton, and its chat composer's attachment X is DraftAttachmentThumbnail's. Only the Mac-only views (MacChatReplyBarLayout, MacReplyIndicator) and ComposeView's Forward strip add names where they use a control. On iOS, the quote X and the selection checkbox have no name and no selected trait. The conversation row is several elements, not one, with a tap gesture and no declared traits.

**Evidence**

- esc-chatmail/Views/Components/SendButton.swift:15-31 — a Button whose label is Image(systemName: "arrow.up"), with no accessibilityLabel anywhere in the component
- esc-chatmail/Platform/MacMailboxView.swift:120-123 — the Mac presents ComposeView(mode: .newMessage); ComposeViewModel.swift:151-155 sets showSubjectField false for .newMessage, so ComposeView.swift:120-121 shows ComposeInputBar, whose line 100 draws the unlabeled SendButton on the Mac too
- esc-chatmail/Views/Compose/ChatReplyBar.swift:208 — the Mac's floating composer uses DraftAttachmentThumbnail, whose remove Button (DraftAttachmentThumbnail.swift:45-51) is an xmark.circle.fill image with no name; only ComposeView.swift:107 names it, for the Forward strip
- esc-chatmail/Platform/MacChatReplyBarLayout.swift:119,142 and MacReplyIndicator.swift:33-34 — the Mac-only emoji, send and quote-drop buttons are named ("Emoji and symbols", "Send", "Don’t quote this message")
- esc-chatmail/Views/Compose/ChatReplyBarHeaderRow.swift:101-106 — the iOS quote-drop Button is an xmark.circle.fill image with no accessibilityLabel
- esc-chatmail/Views/Main/ConversationListView.swift:89-102,208-219 — the row is an HStack with onTapGesture (ConversationRowView.swift:124-215 declares no accessibilityElement, label or trait), and the selection Button is a circle or checkmark image with no label and no isSelected trait

**Trigger.** VoiceOver or Voice Control on iOS when replying in a chat, removing a draft attachment, dropping a quote, selecting rows or opening a conversation. On the Mac: the New Message sheet's send button and the chat composer's attachment remove button.

**Impact.** The primary Send button is spoken and offered to Voice Control under the arrow symbol's name, not "Send", on both platforms' New Message and on the iOS chat reply. The remove and drop-quote controls get the generic xmark name. The selection state can be told only from the symbol and the navigation title's count. Each row is read as several separate texts. The controls still work, through the symbol name or Voice Control's numbers, so this is a degradation, not a block. Each new use site of a shared component inherits the missing name, which is how the Mac sheet got it.

**Verifier.** Every cited line matches the code. The finding says the Mac counterparts are labeled, and that is wrong for two of the four controls: the shared SendButton and DraftAttachmentThumbnail are also unlabeled on the Mac. The Mac sidebar does get native selection from List(selection:). No document records this as a deliberate decision. What VoiceOver and Voice Control do with onTapGesture rows and symbol-derived names is platform behavior that this code cannot show. Medium fits as structural debt; it is arguably low.

**October review.** No scalability-review item. The only related prior work is CLAUDE.md's "The word an empty message field shows" (MessageFieldPolicy, MessageFieldSourceTests), and mac-imessage-ui-plan.md:265 covers only the filter button.

**Invariant risks**

- The PR #182 rule at ConversationListView.swift:80-88 says Select and normal mode share one structural path. Row traits must be values passed to modifiers that are always applied. An if/else, or a Button wrapped around the row, would rebuild every visible row when Select is toggled.
- Wrapping the row in a Button is unsafe. The standard palette leaves the title color nil (ConversationRowView.swift:160-162), so a List button's tint would recolor the name. Two buttons in one row fire together unless each is .plain. The .iOS row is checked by drawing it before and after a change.
- Every send goes through ChatReplyBar.sendIfAllowed behind canSend. A VoiceOver magic-tap or custom action must call that path, never onSend directly. A custom remove action must not bypass allowsDraftMutation or .disabled.
- ConversationRowView is shared with the Mac sidebar's List(selection:) table row, so .isButton and .combine belong at the iOS call site. New source pins read files through repositorySource(_:), not a private #filePath reader.

**Fix.** Change labels only and add no new routes. 1. Inside SendButton add .accessibilityLabel("Send"). Inside DraftAttachmentThumbnail, name the remove Button "Remove <filename>" and delete the outer label at ComposeView.swift:107. Also name RecipientChip's X and ChatView's ellipsis Menu. 2. Make "Don’t quote this message" one constant in ReplyIndicatorPolicy, read by both ChatReplyBarHeaderRow's X and MacReplyIndicator. 3. For the iOS row, change ConversationListView's call site only. Add .accessibilityElement(children: .combine) and traits from a pure ConversationRowAccessibilityPolicy: isButton, plus isSelected while selecting. Give unread and pinned as the accessibility value. Add a default accessibility action that calls the same activateRow function as onTapGesture, and hide the selection button from accessibility. Never wrap the row in a Button.

**First step.** Name the buttons inside SendButton and DraftAttachmentThumbnail, remove the outer label at ComposeView.swift:107, and add the source pins. Then build iOS and the unsigned Mac --for-testing target, because Swift 6.2 and 6.4 differ.

**Pinning test.** A default-plan AccessibilityNameSourceTests read through repositorySource(_:), asserting each named Button's modifier chain has its label, with a Revert-check per site. Add ConversationRowAccessibilityPolicyTests for the traits and value. HONEST SCOPE: a test host cannot read SwiftUI's accessibility.

**Payoff.** VoiceOver and Voice Control users get "Send", "Remove <file>", the selection state and one element per conversation on both platforms. Shared components stop passing the missing names to new call sites.

### `gap-accessibility-architecture#3` · low · maintainability · effort S · new

**Style values take only the platform as input: card and compose text ignores Dynamic Type, and colors ignore Increase Contrast**

Area: Accessibility under a virtualized transcript and fixed-height layout contracts. Verdict: corrected (medium confidence).

The cards' fixed sizes are a documented decision, and the failure the auditor describes is the cost that decision already accepts. Beyond it, the real gaps are small. Three iOS inputs use fixed sizes that ignore Dynamic Type: New Message's body (18pt), the To field (18pt) and the list's search field (17pt). The bubble text and the chat reply field already scale. The bubble fills are system colors, not literals. What does not adapt is the forwarded card's white text at 0.82 and 0.66 opacity on sent bubbles, roughly 3.2:1 and 2.6:1 in default settings.

**Evidence**

- esc-chatmail/Views/Components/EmailPreview/EmailPreviewCardMetrics.swift:20-21,76-78 — the file says the sizes 'are fixed points and do not follow Dynamic Type' so a card's height is known at mount; font(_:_:) returns .system(size:)
- CLAUDE.md:170 — 'The sizes stay fixed points, not text styles, so a card's height is known when its row mounts' (deliberate; EmailPreviewCardMetricsTests pins .iOS field by field)
- esc-chatmail/Views/Compose/ComposeInputBar.swift:87 — the body font is .system(size: 18) only for the .iMessage presentation, otherwise .body; ComposeView.swift:42-43 uses .iMessage only for mode == .newMessage
- esc-chatmail/Views/Compose/RecipientInputSection.swift:71,110 and Views/Main/ConversationListView.swift:349 — the 'To:' label and the recipient TextField are .system(size: 18); the search TextField is .system(size: 17)
- esc-chatmail/Views/Compose/ChatReplyBar.swift:124 with Views/Components/PlaceholderTextField.swift:11 — the chat reply field takes the default textFont .body, so it scales; MessageContentView.swift:188-193 — the bubble Text sets no font (.body)
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ForwardedMessageCard.swift:96-105 — on sent bubbles, secondary and tertiary text are Color.white.opacity(0.82/0.66) over a white 0.14 card fill; MessageBubbleStyle.swift:105-118 — the bubble fills are .blue, Color.gray.opacity(0.2) and systemGray5 (system colors, not literals)

**Trigger.** An iOS user with a larger or accessibility text size who uses New Message or search; any user viewing a forward they sent.

**Impact.** At accessibility sizes, text typed in New Message (To and body) and in the list's search stays at 17-18pt while the rest of the app grows. The forwarded card's 'To:' and timestamp lines on the user's own sent forwards fall below 4.5:1 contrast for 11-13pt text. The cards not following Dynamic Type is the accepted cost of a documented decision.

**Verifier.** Every cited line is present. The card part is a documented decision (file header and CLAUDE.md), and its failure is the stated cost. The auditor's argument against the rationale is reasonable (dynamicTypeSize is known at mount, and the drive card's comment says its height would still hold), but it is not a concrete failure beyond that cost. 'Colors are literals' overstates it: .blue, .gray, .primary and .secondary are system colors (not measured under Increase Contrast). The Mac collapses high contrast on purpose (PlatformColor.swift:35-37). The chat reply field scales.

**October review.** CLAUDE.md:170 (card sizes stay fixed points, deliberate) and EmailPreviewCardMetrics.swift:20-21; nothing in docs/scalability-review.md (no accessibility, Dynamic Type or contrast item)

**Invariant risks**

- Card heights must be known when the row mounts (EmailPreviewCardMetrics.swift:20-21, CLAUDE.md:170, AGENTS.md:139). Scaling fonts inside the fixed date tile (70x92), NewsletterPreviewCard's frame(height: 142) or the cards' minimum heights clips text or resizes a mounted row. The shared-file skeleton bar is also sized from linkTitleSize (GoogleDriveSharedFileCardView.swift:145-155).
- Tests pin the .mac card metrics as no larger than the iPhone's and at most 13pt (EmailPreviewCardMetricsTests:54-102). Both the metrics and those tests run in Mac.xctestplan, so using UIFontMetrics or UITraitCollection there breaks CI's macOS build.
- Tests pin the .standard bubble colors value by value (MessageBubbleStyleTests:30-33). standard.recipientBubbleColor() is also the image backdrop (ImageBackdropPolicy.swift:69, ImageBackdropPolicyTests:592), and the .mac fill must stay opaque under the tail (MessageBubbleStyle.swift:116-118). Replacing Color.gray.opacity(0.2) breaks all three and fixes no contrast gap.
- The iMessage To row has a fixed frame(height: 52) (RecipientInputSection.swift:80), and the Mac's New Message sheet uses the same compose style (MacMailboxView.swift:121-123). Scaling the font there without changing it to minHeight clips the To field at accessibility sizes.

**Fix.** Make two small changes that move no transcript row, and leave card sizing alone, which CLAUDE.md:170 records as a decision. 1) Contrast: add a pure ForwardedMessageCardPalette chosen by isFromMe and @Environment(\.colorSchemeContrast). Its standard case equals today's literals. Its increased case gives sent cards opaque white secondary and tertiary text and drops the white overlay fill. 2) Dynamic Type: the To label and field and the New Message body take @ScaledMetric(relativeTo: .body) of 18. The search field takes .body, and the iMessage To row's frame(height: 52) becomes a minHeight. At the default text size nothing changes on screen. Do not touch the bubble fills, .mac or EmailPreviewCardMetrics; scaling the cards is a separate decision for Kevin.

**First step.** Add ForwardedMessageCardPalette next to ForwardedMessageCard.swift, with a standard and an increased case for each isFromMe. Its standard values copy lines 92-110 exactly. The card then reads colorSchemeContrast to pick a case.

**Pinning test.** ForwardedMessageCardPaletteTests: standard is pinned field by field to today's literals (Revert-check), and the increased case's sent secondary and tertiary colors are opaque white. A source test pins that the three typed-text fields use @ScaledMetric or .body and that the To row uses minHeight.

**Payoff.** Under Increase Contrast, the secondary lines of a forward the user sent become legible. New Message and search text grow with the user's text size. No transcript row's height changes.

### `gap-accessibility-architecture#4` · low · reliability · effort S · new

**The transcript's bottom and inset contracts ignore Dynamic Type: a mid-chat size change strands the reader, and the composer cap is in lines**

Area: Accessibility under a virtualized transcript and fixed-height layout contracts. Verdict: corrected (medium confidence).

The mechanism holds on iOS. A revealed transcript anchors size changes at the top. Once the bounded follow has expired (usually about 3 s after the last growth, 30 s at most), growth that pushes the bottom anchor offscreen goes unanswered. A larger text size grows the rows and the composer, so a reader who was at the bottom has the newest message pushed under the composer. Latest-following then turns off until they scroll or focus the field. The top of the viewport stays put, so the reader keeps their place. The 5-line field cap is a bounded limit on the user's own draft.

**Evidence**

- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ChatTranscriptScrollAnchorPolicy.swift:59-61 — sizeChanges returns .top once isTranscriptRevealed
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ChatMessagesCoordinator.swift:878-882 — with the follow .inactive, a geometry update falls through to `guard case .pending` and returns; follow grace 3 s (184), lifetime cap 30 s (207, 2326-2331)
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ChatMessagesCoordinator.swift:1453 — a count change scrolls only if isBottomAnchorVisible; ChatMessagesView.swift:911 sets setFollowsLatestInsertions(isVisible)
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ChatMessagesCoordinator.swift:1546-1573 — the comment names 'late bubble growth after the follow expired' as a known off-bottom state; a keyboard show then scrolls to the bottom (the self-heal)
- esc-chatmail/Views/Chat/ChatView.swift:339-355 with ChatBottomInsetPolicy.swift:261-270 — composer growth is compensated only while the scene is active (or the field is focused), so not from behind Control Center
- esc-chatmail/Views/Components/PlaceholderTextField.swift:8,34 vs ReplyIndicatorPolicy.swift:116-123 — the field is capped at 5 lines of the user's own text; the 120 pt header cap exists because a sender's Reply-To list is unbounded

**Trigger.** On iOS, with a chat open at the bottom, the user raises the Dynamic Type size (Control Center or Settings) after the post-reveal follow has expired. That is usually a few seconds after the last growth, not only after 30 s.

**Impact.** The newest message slides partly or wholly under the composer, and new arrivals stop auto-scrolling into view. One scroll down or a tap on the reply field fixes it. Nothing is lost, and the top of what the reader was viewing stays in place. At accessibility sizes a full 5-line draft makes the composer tall, but it is bounded and the content is the user's own.

**Verifier.** Confirmed: dynamicTypeSize is read only in MessageBubble (git grep), and nothing observes size-category changes. This is one more instance of the uncorrected late growth after the follow's bounded lifetime, which the code accepts and names (1550-1552). The claim that the reader 'loses their place' is overstated: the .top anchor keeps the top of the viewport. The two heal paths (keyboard show at 1567, unfocus at 1601) were missed. The composer-cap half is not the header's failure mode. Not run.

**Invariant risks**

- Bounded follow: an expired follow must stay deaf to ordinary growth. testPostRevealBottomFollowExpiresAfterGracePeriod pins this (ChatMessagesCoordinatorTests.swift:896-903), as do the 3 s grace and 30 s cap at ChatMessagesCoordinator.swift:184 and 207. A 'stick to the bottom whenever last seen there' fix breaks that test and brings back the endless follow the cap exists to stop.
- Each follow's state lives only in the PostRevealBottomFollowState/BottomFollow cases (CLAUDE.md Traps, ChatMessagesCoordinator). A new stored 'wasAtBottomBeforeTextSizeChange' flag on the coordinator is exactly the hand-reset state that trap forbids.
- The hidden pass owns scrolling until the reveal. A follow armed while initialRevealState is .pending catches every geometry report before the reveal machine sees it (ChatMessagesCoordinator.swift:1384-1390). A compensated-shift hold's settle check owns the anchor while it is in flight (1205-1225), so the handler must not start a competing scroll.
- Never yank a reader out of history. Only the 2 pt drag sets the takeover (ChatMessagesView.swift:479-482, 948-953). A trackpad or a likely VoiceOver scroll does not set it, so require that the anchor was visible, not just that no takeover is active. The 'restore the topmost row' half would be a programmatic history scroll that moves the virtual window outside its holds. The composer must stay the overlay whose measured height is the inset (ChatComposerStyleSourceTests).

**Fix.** Add one coordinator entry, handleTextSizeChange(scrollAction:), called from ChatMessagesView's onChange(of: dynamicTypeSize) on iOS. Guard it like the keyboard and focus handlers: .ready, initial window loaded, visible, no takeover, no finger down, no user-driven scroll phase, and the bottom anchor visible in the report before the change. Then arm a fresh bounded follow, the armPostSendBottomFollow shape, with its state only in the follow cases. If the growth report already pushed the anchor off, request one unanimated requestPostRevealBottomScroll. Expired follows stay deaf to plain growth. Drop the 'restore the topmost row' half. Optionally, in a separate change, give the reply field fewer lines at accessibility sizes through a pure line-limit policy, rather than a frame sized as a share of the viewport.

**First step.** On the iOS simulator, use a throwaway diagnostic and `simctl ui content_size` to measure whether onChange(of: dynamicTypeSize) fires before or after the geometry report that carries the growth. That order decides which visibility reading the handler can trust.

**Pinning test.** ChatMessagesCoordinatorTests: reveal, expire the follow (now += 3.1), report anchor visible, call the new handler, report growth with anchor offscreen, expect exactly one post-reveal layout scroll. Takeover and pending-pass variants scroll nothing. Revert-check: the handler's follow arm.

**Payoff.** Readers at the bottom who change text size keep the newest message above the composer, and new mail keeps auto-scrolling into view. Small accessibility gain, no data or performance impact.

### `gap-accessibility-architecture#6` · low · maintainability · effort M · known-open

**Nothing can verify accessibility: there is no UI test target, off-screen drawings cannot see the accessibility tree, and VoiceOver has never been heard**

Area: Accessibility under a virtualized transcript and fixed-height layout contracts. Verdict: corrected (medium confidence).

The gap is real but overstated. The tests do check the app's accessibility decisions where they are policy or source: label, hint and value strings (FailedSendRecoveryPolicy, MacSidebarFilterBadgePolicy), modifiers pinned in source, the Mac reply text view's AppKit label (read in two suites), and Dynamic Type layout and arrangement. What nothing checks is what SwiftUI builds from them: traits, grouping, reading order, contrast, clipping, and what VoiceOver says. The test host sees no SwiftUI accessibility tree. There is no UI test target, so performAccessibilityAudit cannot run, and the plan docs' manual VoiceOver checks are still open.

**Evidence**

- CLAUDE.md:150 — no UI test target; the never-run esc-chatmailUITests and the UI_TEST_MODE / UI_TEST_AUTHENTICATED hooks were removed (commit ea41dfd5, which also removed a path that forced isAuthenticated = true)
- esc-chatmailTests/Platform/MessageFieldSourceTests.swift:15-20 — nothing asks SwiftUI what it tells VoiceOver: the hosting views answered accessibilityChildren()/accessibilityElements with none, and VoiceOver has not been heard on either platform
- esc-chatmailTests/Chat/MessageSendStatusLinePolicyTests.swift:142-147 — the accessibility-size arrangement is pinned as a policy decision only; the view wiring is unchecked 'with no UI test target'
- esc-chatmailTests/Chat/FailedSendRecoveryPolicyTests.swift:37-46 — accessibility hint strings are pinned at the policy level
- esc-chatmailTests/Platform/MacChatReplyBarLayoutTests.swift:139 — a second AppKit accessibilityLabel() read besides MacReplyTextFieldTests:480,493
- docs/mac-imessage-ui-plan.md:275 — VoiceOver on the filter badge is listed under 'Not seen: check in the signed, sandboxed app', still open

**Trigger.** A UI change that alters SwiftUI's accessibility tree (traits, grouping, order, contrast, clipping) and leaves the pinned policy strings and source lines as they are.

**Impact.** SwiftUI-level accessibility regressions on iOS and the Mac can reach TestFlight unnoticed. No concrete accessibility defect is shown. The App Store 'Dark Interface' label claim has no basis anywhere in the repository.

**Verifier.** The mechanism checks out: there is no UI test target in project.pbxproj (only application and unit-test product types), and no XCUIApplication or performAccessibilityAudit anywhere. Corrections: 'Nothing can verify accessibility' is too strong (policy strings, source pins, two AppKit label reads, Dynamic Type at .accessibility3 and the accessibility-size arrangement policy are all checked). The App Store impact is not grounded. Severity is lowered to low because the gap is already documented, is shared by every UI area of the app, and comes with no demonstrated failure.

**October review.** CLAUDE.md:150 (no UI test target; UI_TEST_MODE hooks removed in ea41dfd5) and CLAUDE.md:172 (VoiceOver not heard on either platform); docs/mac-imessage-ui-plan.md:275, :352 (VoiceOver checks open), :606 (Mac UI checked manually, app never launched). Not in docs/scalability-review.md.

**Invariant risks**

- Bringing back the removed forced-auth hook (ea41dfd5 set `authSession.isAuthenticated = true`) would show the signed-in UI without going through any of AuthSession's sign-in paths. It skips close, quiesce and reopen, `prepareLocalStoreForAuthenticatedAccount` and `pendingActionAuthenticationDidRecover`. `canAccessMailbox` becomes true, so `handleAuthStateChange` starts sync and pending actions with no token (AuthSession.swift:260-269, esc_chatmailApp.swift:409-418).
- A Mac UI test launches the app as an ordinary process: XCTest is not loaded in it (RuntimeEnvironment.swift:8-12), so neither `MacUnitTestHostGuard` nor the throwaway store applies (CoreDataStack.swift:165-171). The app would open the real container it shares with the installed TestFlight MushMail, restore the real session and could migrate the real store. Built unsigned it runs unsandboxed, and its cleanup deletes ~/Documents/Messages.
- Seeding at the default URL, or on a second model, breaks things: two NSManagedObjectModels in one process break `+[NSManagedObject entity]`. Overriding through `Dependencies(coreDataStack:)` only partly works, because PendingActionsManager, SyncEngine and PersonCache stay on `.shared` (Dependencies.swift:368-389). Redirect the shared stack's store URL instead. Seed text-only rows, so no body file is written outside HTMLContentHandler.
- Wiring and shipping: Xcode Cloud archives the Release configuration on every merge (the scheme's ArchiveAction is Release), so the flag must be inside `#if DEBUG`. Never hand-edit project.pbxproj. `run-tests.sh` refuses `-testPlan`, so the new plan needs its own flag, and that flag must refuse a Mac DESTINATION. Keep it out of the default plan and out of CI's blocking job.

**Fix.** iOS simulator only. Behind `#if DEBUG && targetEnvironment(simulator)` and one launch argument, the app enters an audit mode. That mode never runs `initializeApp()` (no fresh-install cleanup, restore, sync, pending actions or BGTask arming) and never sets `isAuthenticated`. `CoreDataStack.persistentContainer` redirects the store to a temporary directory, next to the existing Mac unit-test-host branch, so every `.shared` service sees one seeded, text-only store on the one model. The audit root mounts the real `ConversationListView`, `ChatView` and `ComposeView`. A UI test target, added in Xcode, runs `performAccessibilityAudit` on each screen at the default and AX sizes, light and dark, through `codex-test.sh --accessibility`, which refuses macOS. The Mac stays a scripted manual VoiceOver pass.

**First step.** Write the app-side code first, with no new target: the DEBUG-and-simulator launch argument, the store redirect beside `makeUnitTestHostStoreURL`, skipping `initializeApp`, and the two pinning tests in the default plan. Then Kevin adds the UI target in Xcode.

**Pinning test.** A default-plan source test (via `repositorySource`) pinning that audit mode sits under `#if DEBUG && targetEnvironment(simulator)`, never sets `isAuthenticated` and skips `initializeApp`. A store-URL test that audit mode never opens the default URL. Plus the audit UI tests.

**Payoff.** Catches SwiftUI-level accessibility regressions (missing labels and traits, clipping at accessibility sizes, contrast, hit regions) on the iOS list, chat and New Message before TestFlight, with no forced-auth path.

## Refuted

- **ESCChatmail 7 is the first non-additive model version, and the stack can only run an inferred lightweight migration, on the main actor** (`data-model`): Read CoreDataStack, AppStartupBootstrap, the error classifier and recovery handler, the rollup snapshot and routing policy; diffed all six model versions. Every step 10 schema change (added attributes, index adds and drops, an inverse removal) is within inferred lightweight migration. The auditor's own fix is an app-level backfill, not a staged migration. Migration errors deleting the store (CoreDataErrorClassifier.swift:128) is the documented ladder, guarded by a migration test per version (V3 to V6 suites exist).
- **Multi-account is precluded structurally: there is one slot for every account-scoped thing** (`account-boundary-auth`): I opened every cited location, and the mechanism is as described (76 files declare `static let shared`). The finding's own note says it is not a defect and that the single store is a recorded decision. CLAUDE.md records the single store and the policy that a sign-out wipes and sign-in starts fresh (Kevin, 2026-11-16). The scalability item for O(n) sign-out unlinks has been built (tombstones). The "full re-sync" claim overstates the cost: the next sign-in syncs from the moment of sign-in. No concrete failure goes beyond the accepted cost.
- **About thirty suites pin behaviour by matching production source text, standing in for seams that do not exist** (`testing-ci-release`): I checked the counts by grep. 31 files read source, as claimed. Corrected counts: 20 of the 23 *SourceTests read source (105 tests, not 119). ChatForward, MessageBubbleContent and FullEmailReaderWarmWidth are behavioural tests. There are 23 hand-written walk-up sites, not 29. CLAUDE.md:143 documents the practice. The fix suggests a blocking lint step, which conflicts with CLAUDE.md:44 (lint is advisory). CLAUDE.md:150 records that the UI test target was removed. That Xcode Cloud has no test action comes from the user's notes; the repository cannot show it.
- **The initial sync window and the mailbox start trust the device clock, so the 30-day cap cannot bound a slow clock** (`gap-wall-clock-time`): I traced every stamp site. FreshInstallHandler disconnects any old Google session, so the next sign-in is interactive and re-stamps the start. performDurableLocalCleanup's stamp at sign-out is likewise overwritten by the next interactive sign-in. One residual path is not gated by the token check: a restore that finds another account's store resets it and stamps the start with no skew limit, and the Core Data recovery ladder reaches back 30 days plus any skew. Both also need a skewed clock to survive token refreshes, which GIDGoogleUser.m:151 sends through the same validating call. That only applies if Google returns an ID token on refresh, which I did not verify. It would be a separate, rare finding.
- **The conversation key is the exact address set with no size threshold, so large recurring mailings fork a chat per mailing** (`gap-message-shape-extremes`): I read the identity, router, serializer, factory and participant persister. The hash and the lack of a threshold are as the finding says. The finding still fails on three points. Its "per mailing" impact is wrong, because identical sets reuse the conversation. Forking when the recipient set changes is documented on purpose: the router doc says so, and the split migration retired gmThreadId grouping. The recommendation to key by sender plus Gmail thread would reverse that decision. Fork frequency at large group sizes was never measured. At most this is a product-policy question, not a scalability defect.

## Dropped as recorded decisions

- **Layering is a folder convention in one 138k-line target: services reach up into views and the sync core references about twenty sibling subsystems** (`di-modularity`): deliberate-decision: docs/mac-app-plan.md:7-9 Summary, 'One target, two platforms' (sync, send and persistence shared as they are); docs/archive/consolidation.md:389-391 non-goal 'DI overhaul' (ratchet, not a rewrite); CLAUDE.md Conventions 'DI'. Not in docs/scalability-review.md. Do not extract packages now: the one-target layout is a recorded decision, gains are unmeasured, and the 'near-leaf' text package is not a leaf (ForwardedMessageDisplayParser.swift:308,327 reach Contacts and Send; ParsedEmail.swift:83,121 reach HTMLContent and Preview; it holds two account-boundary participants). Ins
- **`Dependencies` is a façade over 78 singletons: injection is opt-out per parameter, partly dead, and yields hybrid graphs** (`di-modularity`): deliberate-decision: CLAUDE.md Conventions "**DI:**" (line 131: default-valued `.shared` parameters are house style) and Testing (line 148: "there is no automatic global reset"); no matching item in docs/scalability-review.md Keep default-`.shared` injection, the documented convention. Do not strip defaults from the sync, send or auth cores, and do not build a second graph. Fix only the dead seams. Delete `Dependencies.keychainService` and `remoteConfigProvider`: both are stored, never read, and never passed by any caller. Give `IncrementalSyncOrchestrator` a `remoteConfig: any RemoteConfigPro

## Areas the completeness critic named

- **MIME body decoding fidelity and internationalized mail** (audited): No auditor owned the step from MIME bytes to text. Every body is read as UTF-8, and the bytes are thrown away once decoded, so mail from Outlook in windows-1252 and from Japanese, Chinese, Korean or Russian senders can be stored garbled for good, with no way to re-materialize it. Content loss for ordinary senders is critical-to-high for a mail client. On top of that, the decoding is guessed in four places and the canonical hash parses addresses differently from the rows. A senior architect would not sign off on a mail client whose charset handling has never been tested.
- **iPad and iOS 17.6-25: devices and OS versions the app ships to and nothing runs** (audited): Xcode Cloud ships every merge to iPad and to iOS 17.6 devices, and nothing has ever built a plan for, tested or measured either. The layout code reads the screen rather than the window, so composers and bubbles can be wrong in ordinary iPad multitasking. That is a user-visible failure under common conditions on a platform no auditor was given.
- **From one store save to every observer: merge, cache invalidation and UI** (audited): Each UI auditor measured their own observer. Nobody owns the sum, or the order between the merge and the cache invalidation, on the path every new message and every action takes. A severe main-thread cost at S2 is therefore likely and has never been measured; medium-to-high.
- **The device's wall clock is the only clock: clock changes, skew and time zones** (audited): Clocks are commonly wrong (dead battery, travel, manual change, restore), and no auditor owned time. A cursor computed from a future time can skip mail for good, and a shield from a future time can block server changes indefinitely. Medium.
- **Message structure the sender controls, beyond HTML: recipients, MIME tree, part and attachment counts** (audited): Content-pipeline bounded HTML size and DOM depth, and attachments-storage-disk found the crash on image size. No one bounded message structure, which the sender fully controls and which feeds the conversation key, the store and main-thread views. That leaves open crashes and degradation a stranger can trigger by sending one message; medium-to-high.
- **Accessibility under a virtualized transcript and fixed-height layout contracts** (audited): The layout contracts the transcript's correctness depends on (heights fixed at mount, a sliding window of realized rows, a hidden reveal pass) are exactly the ones assistive technologies break. No auditor examined them, and the code base itself records that nobody has ever heard VoiceOver on it. Medium: the cost is structural, not cosmetic.
- **Growth over a process's life, and in-memory state that ignores the account** (not audited): mac-platform covered the policy side of a process that lives for days (latches). The resource side, and stores that are not participants and so are invisible to an audit that starts from the boundary's hooks, belong to no one. Low-to-medium, but growing linearly on the platform the author uses every day.

(4) CLAUDE.md:37's ship-gate claim rests on an App Store Connect setting the repo cannot show.
